Read "The problem", "Theory" and "In the project". The trade-offs section *(deep dive)* compares fakes, mocks and snapshot tests.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: inspecting a building"}
A new building is inspected at several levels. Each steel beam is tested in a lab (cheap, fast, precise). Each floor is checked as it's built: do the beams, pipes and wiring fit together? And before anyone moves in, the whole building is walked through once. Nobody inspects only beams, and nobody waits for the walk-through to find a bad beam.

A test suite works the same way. Its strategy is the choice of how much to inspect at each level, and how to know the inspections themselves are any good.
:::

## The problem

Atlas has had tests since lesson 4.5, and by now there are many: 124 at the start of this lesson, all passing. Does that mean Atlas works? This course has already met three cases where a green suite was wrong:

- **Lesson 4.3**: `PATCH /users/me` with `null` crashed with a 500. No test sent `null`.
- **Lesson 4.17**: removing `selectinload(Issue.repo)` broke `GET /issues/{id}` in production, but every test passed, because the tests' session still held the repository in memory.
- **Lesson 4.2**: a test for a secret leak passed while the leak was still there, because Pydantic shortened the value it was searching for.

And here's a fourth, from this lesson. **Coverage** is the share of the code's lines that the tests actually run. The first measurement of Atlas:

```text
src/atlas/api/routes/auth.py         118     41    65%   51, 73-74, 89-98, 100, 115-141, 155-156, 161, 221-240
...
TOTAL                               1281    181    86%
```

It says the refresh route, lines 115 to 141, never runs in any test. But `test_refresh_rotates_tokens` exercises exactly that route, and passes. The measuring tool itself was wrong, for a reason this lesson explains.

So the questions for a test suite aren't "how many?" or "is it green?". They are: does each test check something that matters, at the cheapest level that can catch it? Would it fail if the code broke? And what does nothing test at all?

## Theory

### Levels of test

| Level | What it runs | Speed | Catches | In Atlas |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Unit** | one function or type, no database, no HTTP | microseconds | logic and parsing mistakes | `test_schemas.py`, `test_config.py`, `test_search.py`, `test_stats.py` |
| **In-process integration** | the real app over in-memory HTTP, with a real Postgres | milliseconds | wiring, SQL, validation, errors, security rules | `test_api_*.py`, `test_storage.py` |
| **End-to-end** | a deployed system over the network, with a browser | seconds | configuration, networking, the front end | lesson 4.16's browser check; Part 7 checks the deployed site |

The usual advice, the **test pyramid**, is "many unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end". For an API whose logic lives mostly in its database queries and wiring, that advice bends: Atlas's middle layer is fast (the whole suite runs in seconds against a real Postgres) and catches what matters, so most of Atlas's tests live there. Unit tests are for code that stands alone, like domain types and settings.

### Fakes, stubs and mocks

Tests replace things they can't or shouldn't use for real. Three kinds of stand-in:

- A **stub** returns canned answers: "whatever you ask, here's this response".
- A **fake** is a working, simplified implementation that follows the real thing's rules: lesson 4.9's `FakeGitHubSignIn` issues single-use codes tied to their PKCE challenge, as GitHub does.
- A **mock** records how it was called, so a test can assert "this function was called with these arguments".

Atlas's rule: **fake only what crosses the process boundary** (GitHub, and in Part 6 the language model), and nothing of its own. Mocking your own functions tests that the code calls what it calls today: such tests break every time you restructure, and pass when the behaviour is wrong. And a fake must be strict where the real service is: a fake GitHub that accepted any code would have let the PKCE tests pass against broken code.

### Coverage, and what it can't tell you

Coverage answers one question: **which lines did no test run?** That's valuable, because a line no test runs is a line no test checks. It can't say whether the lines that *did* run were checked: a test that calls a route and asserts nothing gives full coverage of that route. So coverage is a map of blind spots, not a score to raise. Projects that set a coverage target tend to get tests written to reach lines rather than to catch bugs.

### Testing the tests: break it on purpose

The direct way to know whether a test can fail is to make the code wrong and watch. This course has done it at every security lesson: removing the dummy hash (4.7), disabling signature checks (4.8), removing `state` and PKCE (4.9), reuse detection (4.10), the user filter on idempotency keys (4.16). Each time, a specific test went red. Tools can do this systematically (**mutation testing**: change a `<` to `<=` or delete a line, run the suite, report the changes no test noticed). Done by hand for the important rules, it's the cheapest way to trust a suite.

### The contract

Some breakage no behaviour test notices: renaming `/users/me/saved-issues` to `/users/me/saved` keeps the route working, under a new name, while breaking every client. The **contract** of an API (its paths, methods and status codes) deserves a test of its own, one that fails on *any* change, so changes happen on purpose and show up in review.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  U["unit tests<br/>types, settings, pure functions"] --> I["in-process integration tests<br/>real app + real Postgres + fake GitHub"]
  I --> C["contract test<br/>paths, methods, status codes"]
  I --> E["end-to-end checks<br/>browser, deployed system (Part 7)"]
  COV["coverage: what does no test run?"] -.-> I
  MUT["break it on purpose:<br/>does a test fail?"] -.-> U & I
```

## In the project

### Coverage, measured correctly

```bash
uv add --dev pytest-cov
```

**pytest-cov** connects the `coverage` tool to pytest. In `pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[tool.coverage.run]
source = ["atlas"]
# Async SQLAlchemy switches between greenlets; without this, code after those switches
# is reported as never run (lesson 4.19).
concurrency = ["greenlet", "thread"]
# Migrations run through Alembic in CI's migration step, not through pytest.
omit = ["*/atlas/migrations/*"]
```

That `concurrency` line is the answer to "The problem". Async SQLAlchemy runs its database work inside **greenlets**: lightweight units of execution that switch back and forth inside one thread (lesson 4.17 mentioned the `greenlet` package). By default, coverage follows one thread's execution and loses track at those switches, so lines that ran were reported as never run. Told about greenlets, it measures correctly:

```text
$ uv run pytest --cov --cov-report=term-missing
Name                               Stmts   Miss  Cover   Missing
----------------------------------------------------------------
src/atlas/api/app.py                  91      1    99%   176
src/atlas/api/deps.py                 35      3    91%   32-33, 59
src/atlas/api/routes/auth.py         118      5    96%   135, 140, 161, 235-236
src/atlas/api/routes/issues.py        43      0   100%
...
src/atlas/cli.py                     239     71    70%   170, 207-212, 215-225, ...
...
TOTAL                               1281     86    93%
124 passed in 13.36s
```

From 86% to 93% with no new tests: check a tool's numbers against what you know before believing them. The `Missing` column is the useful part. Reading it:

- `cli.py` at 70%: the command-line commands that need a real GitHub token or network. Accepted, deliberately: they're thin wrappers around `storage.py` and `github.py`, which are well tested.
- `deps.py` line 59: a valid token for a user who no longer exists. Lesson 4.8's exercise writes that test.
- `auth.py` lines 235 and 236: the GitHub callback's redirect to the web UI, the code that puts tokens in the URL **fragment** so they never reach a server or its logs (lesson 4.9). A security property with no test.

### Red, then green: the gap coverage found

```python
async def test_the_web_ui_gets_tokens_in_the_fragment_only(
    api_settings: ApiSettings,
    async_session: AsyncSession,
    github: FakeGitHubSignIn,
    tmp_path: Path,
) -> None:
    """Found by coverage (lesson 4.19): the redirect to the web UI had no test."""
    settings = api_settings.model_copy(update={"web_dir": str(tmp_path)})
    app = create_app(settings, github_transport=github.transport)

    async def test_session() -> AsyncIterator[AsyncSession]:
        yield async_session

    app.dependency_overrides[get_session] = test_session
    async with browser(app) as client:
        authorize_url, state = await start_sign_in(client)
        code = github.approve(authorize_url)
        response = await client.get("/auth/github/callback", params={"code": code, "state": state})

    location = urlparse(response.headers["location"])
    assert response.status_code == 302
    assert location.path == "/app/"
    # Tokens in the fragment never reach a server or its logs; a query string would.
    assert location.query == ""
    assert {"access_token", "refresh_token"} <= set(parse_qs(location.fragment))
    assert 'atlas_oauth=""' in response.headers["set-cookie"]
```

`model_copy(update=...)` makes a copy of the settings with one field changed; `tmp_path` is a pytest fixture giving each test an empty temporary folder, standing in for the web UI's files. The last assert checks the sign-in cookie is cleared. The test passes against the current code, so, as lesson 4.5 insists, break the code to see it fail. With `?` instead of `#` in the redirect:

```text
E       AssertionError: assert 'access_token...yqSY8l-M2wWYo' == ''
```

### The contract snapshot

`tests/test_api_contract.py`:

```python
"""The API's contract (lesson 4.19): paths, methods and status codes change only on purpose.

Clients are written against these. A renamed path or a removed status code breaks them even
when every other test passes, so the current contract is compared with a committed snapshot.
After a deliberate change, refresh the snapshot and review its diff in the pull request:

    UPDATE_CONTRACT=1 uv run pytest tests/test_api_contract.py
"""

SNAPSHOT = Path(__file__).parent / "api_contract.json"


def contract(app: FastAPI) -> dict[str, dict[str, list[str]]]:
    """Every documented path, its methods, and each method's documented status codes."""
    paths = app.openapi()["paths"]
    return {
        path: {method: sorted(operation["responses"]) for method, operation in methods.items()}
        for path, methods in sorted(paths.items())
    }


def test_the_api_contract_changes_only_on_purpose(api_settings: ApiSettings) -> None:
    current = contract(create_app(api_settings))
    if os.environ.get("UPDATE_CONTRACT") == "1":
        SNAPSHOT.write_text(json.dumps(current, indent=2, sort_keys=True) + "\n")

    expected = json.loads(SNAPSHOT.read_text())

    assert current == expected
```

`app.openapi()` is the same OpenAPI document lesson 4.1 showed at `/openapi.json`. The first run has no snapshot and fails (`FileNotFoundError`); running once with `UPDATE_CONTRACT=1` writes `tests/api_contract.json`, which is committed:

```json
{
  "/auth/login": {
    "post": [
      "200",
      "422"
    ]
  },
  ...
```

Now the "harmless" rename:

```text
E         Omitting 14 identical items, use -vv to show
E         Left contains 1 more item:
E         {'/users/me/saved': {'get': ['200']}}
E         Right contains 1 more item:
E         {'/users/me/saved-issues': {'get': ['200']}}
```

`web/app.js` calls `/users/me/saved-issues`, so that rename would have broken the web UI's "Saved" tab.

The snapshot also shows a weakness honestly: the documented status codes are mostly `200` and `422`. The 401s, 404s and 409s that routes really return aren't declared in the OpenAPI document (lesson 4.14's stretch is about adding them). The contract test protects what's documented, which is one more reason to document it.

### In CI

The CI job runs `uv run pytest -v --cov --cov-report=term-missing`. Coverage is printed, not enforced: a drop is a prompt to read the `Missing` column, not a reason to fail a build. The migration checks from lesson 4.13 run as their own step.

```text
$ uv run pytest -q --cov
...
TOTAL                               1281     83    94%
126 passed in 14.33s
```

## Trade-offs: stand-ins and snapshots *(deep dive)*

| Approach | Good for | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| Real dependency (Postgres) | anything with SQL in it | needs a database in CI (Atlas has one) |
| Fake (`FakeGitHubSignIn`) | external services you can't call from tests | must be kept as strict as the real service |
| Stub (fixed answers) | one-off cases: "GitHub returns 500" | tests only the answer you chose |
| Mock (`unittest.mock`, asserting calls) | checking a call happens at all, when nothing else can observe it | tests the code's shape, not its behaviour; breaks on refactors |
| Snapshot (`api_contract.json`) | contracts and large outputs that must not change by accident | people refresh snapshots without reading the diff |

The timing defence in lesson 4.7 shows a middle path: instead of measuring time (flaky) or mocking (shape), the test replaced one function with a counting wrapper that still called the real one. Wrappers like that observe without changing behaviour.

**Flaky tests**, ones that sometimes fail with no code change, are worse than no tests: people learn to re-run and ignore them. Common causes are real time (`sleep`, timing assertions), shared state between tests, order dependence and real network calls. Atlas avoids each: rolled-back transactions, a fresh app per test, fakes at the network boundary, and counting instead of timing.

## Common mistakes

- **Treating a green suite as proof.** Ask what the tests' setup does that production doesn't (lesson 4.17's session).
- **Chasing a coverage number**: tests that run lines without checking anything.
- **Believing a tool's output without a sanity check**, like the 86% that was really 93%.
- **Mocking your own code**: tests that pass when behaviour is wrong and fail when it's refactored.
- **Loose fakes** that accept anything, so attack tests can't fail.
- **Refreshing snapshots without reading the diff.** The diff is the point.
- **Never seeing a test fail.** Break the code once, on purpose.

## Check yourself

**1.** Why did coverage first report the refresh route as never run, and how could you tell the report was wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Async SQLAlchemy switches greenlets during database calls, and coverage, not told about greenlets, lost track of execution after those switches. It was visibly wrong because a passing test (`test_refresh_rotates_tokens`) calls that route, so its lines must have run. Setting `concurrency = ["greenlet", "thread"]` fixed it.
:::

**2.** Why does Atlas fake GitHub but not Postgres?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Postgres is part of Atlas's own system: its queries, constraints and full-text search are behaviour the tests must check, and a real Postgres is easy to run in CI. GitHub is outside the process: calling it from tests would be slow, flaky, rate-limited and need real accounts. So GitHub is replaced by a strict fake at the network boundary.
:::

**3.** Every route test passes after renaming `/users/me/saved-issues` (once the tests are updated to the new path). Which test fails, and why is it worth having?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The contract snapshot test. The renamed route works, so behaviour tests updated with it pass, but every client calling the old path (including the web UI) breaks. The contract test makes such changes deliberate and visible in review.
:::

## Exercise

Coverage shows `auth.py` line 161 untested: the 404 when GitHub sign-in isn't configured. Write the test, using `api_settings.model_copy(update={"github_client_id": None})` and `assert_standard_error` from lesson 4.14, and check the line disappears from the `Missing` column.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
async def test_github_sign_in_can_be_switched_off(
    api_settings: ApiSettings, async_session: AsyncSession
) -> None:
    settings = api_settings.model_copy(update={"github_client_id": None})
    app = create_app(settings)

    async with browser(app) as client:
        response = await client.get("/auth/github/login", follow_redirects=False)

    assert_standard_error(response, 404, "github_sign_in_disabled")
```
No session override is needed: the route fails before touching the database (`async_session` is only there so the test is skipped without one, like the other API tests). Run with `--cov --cov-report=term-missing` again and 161 is gone from `auth.py`'s list. Not in the reference code.
:::

## Stretch

Do mutation testing by hand on one module: in `src/atlas/security.py`, make five small changes one at a time (for example `==` to `!=` in the token type check, remove `algorithms=[...]`, return `False` from `verify_password`, change the token lifetime to zero, drop the `str()` around `sub`). Run the suite after each and record which tests caught it. Did any change survive?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each change should turn tests red. For example, flipping the type check to `!=` rejects every real access token and accepts refresh-type ones: on the reference code it fails 16 tests, every authenticated route plus `test_forged_tokens_are_rejected[not an access token]`. A change that survives points at a missing test: write it, watch it fail against the mutated code, then restore the code. Automated tools (mutmut is one for Python) do the same across a whole codebase, slowly, which is why they're usually run occasionally rather than on every commit.
:::

## What changed in the project

`pytest-cov` and coverage settings (with greenlet support) in `pyproject.toml`; CI reports coverage; new `tests/test_api_contract.py` and `tests/api_contract.json`; a test for tokens in the sign-in redirect. Commit: `test: Added a contract snapshot, coverage reporting and a test for tokens in the sign-in redirect`.
